summary.title: Let's write a compiler, part 2: A lexer
summary.one_liner: You learn how to write a hand-coded lexer in C for the PL/0 language, covering token types, whitespace and comment skipping, identifiers versus reserved words, and number validation.
keywords: how do i write a compiler
takeaways: Tokens are defined as integer or character token types; symbols use their ASCII character as the type, and identifiers, numbers and reserved words get their own types.
The lexer is a switch on the current character, skipping whitespace first, then dispatching to ident(), number(), comment handling, or symbol handling.
Identifiers and reserved words are read together and then checked against the reserved word list; numbers are validated with OpenBSD strtonum(3).
The lexer tracks line numbers because it is the only stage that reads newlines in the free-form source, and it errors out on the first problem.
The lexer can be extended into a code formatter once tokens are available, and the parser comes in the next part.
summary.summary: This post, part 2 of a compiler series, implements the lexer for the PL/0 language in C. It starts from the PL/0 grammar to list reserved words, symbols, identifiers and numbers, then defines a TOK_ constant for each token type. The lex() function is a switch over the current character that skips whitespace and comments, while ident() and number() read longer tokens. The author adds underscore digit separators for numbers and a debugging parse() function that prints each token with its line number.
